title: TP 01 · Introduction to time series
text:
This report answers Exercises 1–6 of Task 2 in I5TSA — TD/TP 1: Introduction, issued by Dr. Sim Tepmony and Mr. Nhim Malai. Tasks 1 (quiz) and 3 (take-home assignment) are outside the scope of this revision. The TSA package identifies its companion textbook as Cryer and Chan, Time Series Analysis with Applications in R, second edition.
The required plots are followed by evidence-based interpretations. Additional summaries, normal quantile–quantile (Q–Q) plots, and autocorrelation functions (ACFs) are exploratory supplements, not additional handout questions. The textbook exhibits themselves were not supplied: the plots below reproduce the requested series and plotting conventions without claiming an exact graphical facsimile.
Three distinctions guide the analysis:

Time dependence concerns how observations relate across time. Joining points preserves their order but does not imply that intervening values were observed.
Marginal distribution describes values at an individual time: for example, Gaussian, chi-square, or Student’s \(t\). Nonnormality does not imply dependence.
Sample appearance varies between realizations. Short runs, clusters, and extreme observations can occur in an independent process.

title: TP 01 · Introduction to time series
text:
2 Reproducible setup and data audit
The analysis uses base R, TSA for datasets, and knitr for tables. Install project dependencies once with Rscript scripts/setup.R; package installation is deliberately excluded from the report. Render from the project root with quarto render TP01/tp01.qmd. Each simulation has a recorded seed, and the random-number generator is specified explicitly. Session and package versions are reported at the end.


Code
required <- c("TSA", "knitr")
missing <- required[!vapply(required, requireNamespace, logical(1),
                            quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing)) {
  stop("Install the required packages first: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "))
}

# Load datasets without attaching TSA, which also defines statistical functions.
data("larain", package = "TSA")
data("color", package = "TSA")
data("tempdub", package = "TSA")
RNGkind(kind = "Mersenne-Twister", normal.kind = "Inversion",
        sample.kind = "Rejection")
options(digits = 4)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%")

ink <- "#176B87"
accent <- "#A64B00"
fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
lag1 <- function(x) {
  as.numeric(stats::acf(as.numeric(x), lag.max = 1, plot = FALSE)$acf[2])
}

series <- list(larain = larain, color = color, tempdub = tempdub)
stopifnot(
  all(vapply(series, is.ts, logical(1))),
  all(vapply(series, function(x) all(is.finite(x)), logical(1))),
  length(larain) == 115L, frequency(larain) == 1,
  all(start(larain) == c(1878, 1)), all(end(larain) == c(1992, 1)),
  length(color) == 35L, frequency(color) == 1,
  all(start(color) == c(1, 1)), all(end(color) == c(35, 1)),
  length(tempdub) == 144L, frequency(tempdub) == 12,
  all(start(tempdub) == c(1964, 1)), all(end(tempdub) == c(1975, 12))
)




Code
audit <- data.frame(
  Dataset = names(series),
  Observations = vapply(series, length, integer(1)),
  Coverage = c("1878-1992", "Batches 1-35", "Jan 1964-Dec 1975"),
  Index = c("Annual", "Consecutive batches", "Monthly (12/year)"),
  Units = c("Inches", "Color property (unit unspecified)", "Degrees Fahrenheit"),
  Missing = vapply(series, function(x) sum(is.na(x)), integer(1)),
  row.names = NULL
)
knitr::kable(audit)

title: TP 01 · Introduction to time series
section: 3 Exercise 1 · Annual rainfall in Los Angeles
text:
3 Exercise 1 · Annual rainfall in Los Angeles
Question. Plot larain as a time series, corresponding to Exhibit 1.2.


Code
rain_year <- as.numeric(time(larain))
rain_min <- which.min(larain)
rain_max <- which.max(larain)
plot(larain, type = "o", pch = 16, cex = 0.45, col = ink,
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Annual rainfall (inches)",
     ylim = c(0, max(larain) * 1.14),
     main = "Annual rainfall in Los Angeles")
abline(h = mean(larain), col = accent, lty = 2)
text(rain_year[rain_max], larain[rain_max],
     labels = paste(rain_year[rain_max], fmt(larain[rain_max]), "in"),
     pos = 3, cex = 0.8)
text(rain_year[rain_min], larain[rain_min],
     labels = paste(rain_year[rain_min], fmt(larain[rain_min]), "in"),
     pos = 1, cex = 0.8)
legend("topright", "Sample mean", col = accent, lty = 2, bty = "n")








Figure 1: Annual Los Angeles precipitation, 1878–1992. The dashed line is the sample mean, not a fitted trend.







Code
observed_summary <- function(x) {
  c(N = length(x), Mean = mean(x), Median = median(x), SD = sd(x),
    Minimum = min(x), Maximum = max(x), `Lag-1 ACF` = lag1(x))
}
knitr::kable(t(observed_summary(larain)), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)




Table 2: Descriptive statistics of annual rainfall. SD uses the n - 1 denominator.






N
Mean
Median
SD

Lag-1 ACF

Interpretation. Rainfall fluctuates substantially: the observed minimum is 4.08 inches in 1953, and the maximum is 40.29 inches in 1884. The mean (14.89 inches) exceeds the median (14.14 inches), consistent with the influence of unusually wet years. These are extremes relative to this sample; the plot does not establish measurement errors or justify deleting them.
There is no clear sustained monotonic trend in this plot. Because observations are annual totals, within-year seasonality cannot be assessed. The lag-1 sample ACF is -0.033, indicating little observed linear association between adjacent years. A single coefficient, or an absence of obvious visual pattern, does not establish independence, stationarity, or the absence of longer-term climatic variation.

4 Exercise 2 · Industrial color measurements
Question. Plot color, corresponding to Exhibit 1.3.


Code
plot(color, type = "o", pch = 16, cex = 0.65, col = ink,
     xlab = "Consecutive batch number", ylab = "Color property (recorded scale)",
     main = "Color property of an industrial process")
abline(h = mean(color), col = accent, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", "Sample mean", col = accent, lty = 2, bty = "n")








Figure 2: Color property measured in 35 consecutive industrial batches. The dashed line is the sample mean.







Code
knitr::kable(t(observed_summary(color)), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)




Table 3: Descriptive statistics of the industrial color measurements.






N
Mean
Median
SD
Minimum
Maximum
Lag-1 ACF




35

Interpretation. Measurements range from 63 to 87 with mean 74.89. Early batches are generally low, batches 11–18 are mostly higher, batches 19–23 return to lower values, and another high group appears around batches 25–28. These broad movements suggest persistence rather than purely isolated fluctuations. The lag-1 sample ACF is 0.528, appreciably larger than that of rainfall.
Only 35 batches are observed. They do not justify a claim of regular seasonality, a specific cycle length, or an identified change point. The plot motivates investigation of serial dependence and possible process changes without establishing their cause. No engineering tolerance limits are supplied, so these fluctuations cannot be classified as acceptable or unacceptable product quality.

4.1 Supplement · ACFs of the observed series
For lag \(k\), the sample ACF used here is
\[
\widehat\rho(k)=
\frac{\sum_{t=k+1}^{n}(x_t-\bar x)(x_{t-k}-\bar x)}
     {\sum_{t=1}^{n}(x_t-\bar x)^2}.
\]
It describes linear association, not every form of dependence. The dashed limits in Figure 3 are approximate pointwise white-noise reference limits, about \(\pm1.96/\sqrt{n}\). They are not simultaneous limits across all lags and do not constitute a test of independence. Interpretation also presumes a reasonably stable mean and variance; a changing mean can itself produce a large ACF. See the R ACF documentation.


Code
local({
  old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
  on.exit(par(old))
  stats::acf(as.numeric(larain), lag.max = 20,
             main = "Rainfall", xlab = "Lag (years)", col = ink)
  stats::acf(as.numeric(color), lag.max = 10,
             main = "Color", xlab = "Lag (batches)", col = ink)
})








Figure 3: Exploratory ACFs of rainfall and color. Lag units are years and batches, respectively; lag zero is one by definition.

title: TP 01 · Introduction to time series
text:
5 Framework for Exercises 3–5
A completely random process here means independent and identically distributed (iid) observations:
\[
X_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} F,\qquad t=1,\ldots,48.
\]
With finite variance, \(E(X_t)=\mu\), \(\operatorname{Var}(X_t)=\sigma^2\), and \(\operatorname{Cov}(X_t,X_{t-k})=0\) for nonzero \(k\). An iid process is strictly stationary and, with finite variance, weakly stationary. These are properties of the generating model, not conclusions established by inspecting 48 values.
Under the zero-mean convention, weak white noise has zero mean, constant finite variance, and zero autocovariance at nonzero lags. Independence is stronger than being uncorrelated. The normal and \(t_5\) simulations have zero mean; the raw chi-square simulation has mean 2, and its centered version \(X_t-2\) is white noise under this convention.



Model
Mean
Variance
Marginal shape




\(N(0,1)\)
\(0\)
\(1\)
Symmetric, Gaussian


\(\chi^2_2\)
\(2\)
\(4\)
Nonnegative, right-skewed


\(t_5\)
\(0\)
\(5/3\)
Symmetric, heavier tails than Gaussian



We generate three realizations of length 48 per distribution. Each seed is set once before replicate(), allowing the generator state to advance between realizations. Resetting the same seed inside each repetition would reproduce the same path. All generated paths are retained without selecting those that look most persuasive.
The helper displays each realization separately, using common vertical limits within each distribution. A paired normal Q–Q plot examines marginal shape: approximately straight points are compatible with a normal location-scale family, while systematic curvature suggests departures. It cannot diagnose temporal independence. Its line passes through sample quartiles and is not a confidence band.


Code
n <- 48L
B <- 3L

plot_runs <- function(runs, distribution, theoretical_mean) {
  old <- par(mfrow = c(ncol(runs), 2), mar = c(3.6, 4, 2.5, 1),
             mgp = c(2.2, 0.7, 0))
  on.exit(par(old))
  limits <- range(runs, theoretical_mean)
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(runs))) {
    x <- runs[, j]
    plot(seq_along(x), x, type = "o", pch = 16, cex = 0.5,
         col = ink, ylim = limits, xlab = "Time index", ylab = "Value",
         main = paste(distribution, "- realization", j))
    abline(h = theoretical_mean, col = accent, lty = 2)
    stats::qqnorm(x, pch = 16, cex = 0.55, col = ink,
                  ylim = limits, main = paste("Normal Q-Q - realization", j),
                  xlab = "Theoretical normal quantile", ylab = "Sample quantile")
    stats::qqline(x, col = accent, lty = 2)
  }
}

run_summary <- function(runs) {
  data.frame(
    Realization = seq_len(ncol(runs)), N = nrow(runs),
    Mean = colMeans(runs), Variance = apply(runs, 2, var),
    Minimum = apply(runs, 2, min), Maximum = apply(runs, 2, max),
    `Lag-1 ACF` = apply(runs, 2, lag1), check.names = FALSE
  )
}

title: TP 01 · Introduction to time series
text:
6 Exercise 3 · Independent normal observations
Question. Generate 48 independent normal values, plot them, and repeat. Does the series look random?
We choose \(X_t\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,1)\), making the unspecified normal parameters explicit. Thus \(E(X_t)=0\), \(\operatorname{Var}(X_t)=1\), and \(\rho(k)=0\) for \(k\ne0\).


Code
set.seed(2025)
normal_runs <- replicate(B, stats::rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1))
plot_runs(normal_runs, "N(0, 1)", theoretical_mean = 0)








Figure 4: Three standard-normal realizations, each of length 48, with normal Q–Q plots. Horizontal dashed lines mark the theoretical mean of zero.







Code
knitr::kable(run_summary(normal_runs), digits = 3)

Answer. The realizations fluctuate irregularly around zero, and apparent runs or local rises and falls differ between realizations. This appearance is compatible with randomness, but independence is specified by the simulation model, not established by the visual impression. A random process need not alternate signs regularly or have sample mean exactly zero.
Across these realizations, sample means range from -0.338 to 0.128, and sample variances range from 0.892 to 1.034. Such differences reflect sampling variation. The standard deviation of a sample mean is \(1/\sqrt{48}\approx0.144\), so moderate deviations from zero are expected. Q–Q departures at the extremes of a small sample do not, by themselves, establish that the specified normal generator is incorrect.

title: TP 01 · Introduction to time series
text:
7 Exercise 4 · Independent chi-square observations
Question. Repeat with 48 independent chi-square values with two degrees of freedom. Does it look random and nonnormal?
For \(X_t\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\chi^2_2\),
\[
E(X_t)=2,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X_t)=4,\qquad
f(x)=\tfrac12 e^{-x/2}\quad(x>0).
\]
This is an exponential distribution with mean 2 and skewness 2. The R chi-square documentation gives the generator and distribution formulas.


Code
set.seed(2026)
chisq_runs <- replicate(B, stats::rchisq(n, df = 2))
plot_runs(chisq_runs, "Chi-square(2)", theoretical_mean = 2)








Figure 5: Three iid chi-square(2) realizations and normal Q–Q plots. Horizontal dashed lines mark the mean of 2; the raw series has not been centered.







Code

Answer. The timing of high and low observations is irregular, as expected for iid draws. Nonnegative values and occasional large positive spikes reveal asymmetry more readily than in the normal experiment. The maximum over the three retained paths is 11.09; this is a simulation result, not an upper bound on the distribution. Curvature in the normal Q–Q plots helps distinguish this skewed marginal distribution from a Gaussian one.
These paths can look random and nonnormal because the properties concern different aspects of the process. Spikes do not imply serial dependence or data errors. The raw process has a positive mean; \(\varepsilon_t=X_t-2\) is zero-mean iid noise with variance 4. Subtracting 2 changes its location but neither its independence nor its skewness. The standard deviation of the sample mean is \(2/\sqrt{48}\approx0.289\), twice that of the standard-normal experiment.

title: TP 01 · Introduction to time series
text:
8 Exercise 5 · Independent Student’s t observations
Question. Repeat with 48 independent \(t\) values with five degrees of freedom. Does it look random and nonnormal?
For \(X_t\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}t_5\),
\[
E(X_t)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X_t)=\frac{5}{5-2}=\frac53.
\]
The distribution is symmetric with heavier tails than a normal distribution. Its excess kurtosis is \(6/(5-4)=6\), compared with zero for a Gaussian distribution. See the R Student’s t documentation for the generator, density, and mean/variance conditions.


Code
set.seed(2027)
t_runs <- replicate(B, stats::rt(n, df = 5))
plot_runs(t_runs, "Student t(5)", theoretical_mean = 0)








Figure 6: Three iid t(5) realizations and normal Q–Q plots. Horizontal dashed lines mark the theoretical mean of zero.







Code
knitr::kable(run_summary(t_runs), digits = 3)

Answer. As in the normal experiment, paths fluctuate irregularly around zero. The largest observed absolute value across these paths is 9.05. The heavy-tailed model makes large excursions more likely but does not guarantee an obvious extreme in every 48 observations. A short \(t_5\) path may therefore resemble a normal path; nonnormality is less visually apparent than for \(\chi^2_2\).
When sufficiently extreme observations occur, a normal Q–Q plot tends to depart outward in the tails. At this sample size the pattern can be weak or uneven. We know the simulated population is nonnormal from its generating model, not from whether a particular realization passes a visual or formal normality check.
A fair comparison of tails. The raw \(t_5\) distribution also has greater variance than \(N(0,1)\), so larger raw excursions alone do not isolate tail shape. Set \(Z_t=\sqrt{3/5}\,X_t\) to give the \(t\) variable unit variance. Compare the probability of exceeding three population standard deviations in absolute value:


Code
tail_probability <- c(
  2 * stats::pnorm(3, lower.tail = FALSE),
  2 * stats::pt(3 * sqrt(5 / 3), df = 5, lower.tail = FALSE)
)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Distribution = c("Standard normal", "t(5) scaled by sqrt(3/5)"),
  `P(|Z| > 3)` = tail_probability, check.names = FALSE
), digits = 5)




Table 7: Theoretical tail probabilities after matching variance to one; these are not estimates from the 48-point simulations.

This calculation separates heavier tails from the variance difference. The required time plots remain on their original scales; vertical limits are shared within a distribution, not across distributions.

8.1 Supplement · Serial correlation in simulated paths


Code
local({
  old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
  on.exit(par(old))
  examples <- list("N(0, 1)" = normal_runs[, 1],
                   "Chi-square(2)" = chisq_runs[, 1],
                   "Student t(5)" = t_runs[, 1])
  for (nm in names(examples)) {
    stats::acf(examples[[nm]], lag.max = 10, ylim = c(-1, 1),
               main = nm, xlab = "Lag (observations)", col = ink)
  }
})








Figure 7: ACFs of the first realization from each model, selected in advance rather than for its appearance. Limits are approximate pointwise white-noise references.





The population ACF is zero at every positive lag for all three models, but the sample ACF need not be zero. R centers observations when estimating this ACF, including the raw chi-square values. With only 48 observations, the reference limits are approximately $$0.283; isolated crossings can occur by chance, especially when many lags or realizations are inspected. These limits are asymptotic and warrant caution for short, skewed, or heavy-tailed samples. No search for a favorable seed or repeated significance testing is used to certify independence.

title: TP 01 · Introduction to time series
text:
9 Exercise 6 · Monthly temperatures in Dubuque
Question. Plot tempdub with monthly plotting symbols, following the convention in Exhibit 1.9.


Code
month_id <- as.integer(cycle(tempdub))
month_symbol <- substr(month.abb, 1, 1)
local({
  old <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
  on.exit({ layout(1); par(old) })
  layout(matrix(1:2, ncol = 1), heights = c(1, 0.16))
  par(mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
  plot(tempdub, type = "l", col = "grey75", xaxt = "n",
       xlab = "Year", ylab = expression("Monthly average temperature (" * degree * "F)"),
       main = "Monthly temperatures in Dubuque")
  axis(1, at = 1964:1976)
  points(time(tempdub), as.numeric(tempdub),
         pch = month_symbol[month_id], col = ink, cex = 0.75)
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot.new()
  legend("center", legend = month.abb, pch = month_symbol, col = ink,
         ncol = 6, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
})
month_mean <- tapply(as.numeric(tempdub), month_id, mean)
month_sd <- tapply(as.numeric(tempdub), month_id, sd)
coldest <- which.min(month_mean)
warmest <- which.max(month_mean)








Figure 8: Monthly average Dubuque temperatures, January 1964–December 1975, in degrees Fahrenheit. Letters identify months; repeated initials are resolved by calendar position and the legend.





Interpretation. The dominant feature is a strong annual seasonal cycle, with period 12 observations. Temperatures tend to peak in the middle of each calendar year and reach troughs near its beginning and end. Monthly symbols preserve calendar identity, making it easier to compare one January with another rather than with the preceding December alone.
Across the 12 years, the coldest month on average is January (16.61 °F) and the warmest is July (71.72 °F). Their mean difference is 55.11 °F. These are differences between monthly averages across years, not the observed range within every individual year.

9.1 Supplement · Seasonal profile


Code
month_factor <- factor(month_id, levels = 1:12, labels = month.abb)
boxplot(as.numeric(tempdub) ~ month_factor,
        col = "#E4EFF3", border = ink,
        xlab = "Calendar month", ylab = expression("Monthly average temperature (" * degree * "F)"),
        main = "Seasonal profile: 12 observations per calendar month")
lines(1:12, month_mean, type = "b", pch = 16, col = accent)
legend("topleft", "Monthly mean", col = accent, pch = 16, lty = 1, bty = "n")








Figure 9: Temperatures grouped by month across 12 years. Orange points connect monthly means. Boxes display across-year variation, not confidence intervals.

  `Mean (deg F)` = as.numeric(month_mean),

The repeating seasonal mean makes a constant-mean stationary model inappropriate for the raw series. Its lag-1 sample ACF is 0.833, but much of this association can reflect the shared seasonal pattern rather than persistence in temperature anomalies. A later analysis could model calendar-month means or seasonal dynamics and examine residual dependence. Removing estimated seasonality would not automatically establish residual stationarity or independence. This 12-year descriptive plot alone is insufficient to infer a long-term climate trend.

title: TP 01 · Introduction to time series
text:
10 Conclusions
The observed series illustrate annual rainfall variation, persistence in industrial color measurements, and strong annual seasonality in monthly temperatures. The simulations show that independent observations can have Gaussian, skewed, or heavy-tailed distributions. Known population properties must be distinguished from chance features in short realizations. Time plots address temporal structure; Q–Q plots address marginal shape; neither alone proves independence or stationarity.

title: Chapter 1 · Introduction to Time Series
text:
A time series is a sequence of observations \(Y_1, Y_2, \dots, Y_n\) recorded sequentially through time. Unlike classical cross-sectional statistics where observations are assumed to be independent and identically distributed (\(i.i.d.\)), the defining feature of time series is temporal dependence: consecutive or nearby observations are frequently correlated with one another.


According to Cryer and Chan (Chapter 1), the objectives are twofold:

Descriptive & Mechanistic Understanding: To model and understand the underlying stochastic mechanism that generated the observed sequence.
Forecasting: To predict future values \(Y_{n+h}\) based on the series history \(\{Y_1, \dots, Y_n\}\) and other explanatory covariates.




Cryer & Chan emphasize the iterative three-stage modeling cycle proposed by Box and Jenkins (1976):
       ┌───────────────────────────────┐
       │   1. Model Specification      │ <─────────┐
       │   (Tentative Identification)  │           │
       └──────────────┬────────────────┘           │ (Revise if
                      │                            │  inadequate)
                      ▼                            │
       ┌───────────────────────────────┐           │
       │   2. Model Fitting            │           │
       │   (Parameter Estimation)      │           │
       └──────────────┬────────────────┘           │
                      │                            │
                      ▼                            │
       ┌───────────────────────────────┐           │
       │   3. Model Diagnostics        │ ──────────┘
       │   (Residual Checking & Tests) │
       └──────────────┬────────────────┘
                      │ (Adequate model)
                      ▼
       ┌───────────────────────────────┐
       │   Forecasting & Application   │
       └───────────────────────────────┘

Model Specification (Identification): Using visual time plots, sample autocorrelations, and domain knowledge to tentatively select candidate model classes (e.g., AR, MA, ARMA, ARIMA).

Principle of Parsimony: The chosen model should contain the smallest number of parameters that adequately describes the data (“Everything should be made as simple as possible, but not simpler” — Albert Einstein).

Model Fitting (Estimation): Estimating unknown parameters using maximum likelihood or least squares.
Model Diagnostics: Examining model residuals to verify whether assumptions hold (e.g., checking that residuals resemble uncorrelated white noise).

title: Chapter 1 · Introduction to Time Series
text:
2 Setup and Package Initialization
We load the TSA companion package written by Kung-Sik Chan and Jonathan D. Cryer.


Code
library(TSA)

# Ensure reproducible random numbers across R versions
RNGkind(kind = "Mersenne-Twister", normal.kind = "Inversion", sample.kind = "Rejection")

# Graphical palette
primary_col <- "#176B87"
accent_col  <- "#B33939"
point_col   <- "#053B50"
grid_col    <- "#E0E0E0"

title: Chapter 1 · Introduction to Time Series
text:
3 Textbook Case Studies (Section 1.1)
Chapter 1 introduces five historical and industrial time series demonstrating distinct statistical properties:

3.1 Case 1: Annual Rainfall in Los Angeles (larain)
The larain dataset records annual precipitation (in inches) in Los Angeles over more than 100 years (1878–1992).


Code
data(larain)

plot(
  larain,
  ylab = "Inches",
  xlab = "Year",
  type = "o",
  pch = 16,
  col = primary_col,
  main = "Annual Rainfall in Los Angeles"
)
grid(col = grid_col)








Figure 1: Exhibit 1.1: Annual precipitation recorded in Los Angeles, California (1878–1992).





To examine whether consecutive years are statistically dependent, we construct the lag-1 scatterplot (\(Y_t\) versus \(Y_{t-1}\)) using zlag().


Code
plot(
  y = larain,
  x = zlag(larain),
  ylab = "Current Year Rainfall (inches)",
  xlab = "Previous Year Rainfall (inches)",
  pch = 19,
  col = point_col,
  main = "LA Rainfall vs. Previous Year"
)
grid(col = grid_col)
abline(h = mean(larain), v = mean(larain), lty = 2, col = "gray50")

# Compute lag-1 sample autocorrelation
r1_larain <- cor(larain[-1], zlag(larain)[-1])








Figure 2: Exhibit 1.2: Scatterplot of current year rainfall versus previous year rainfall.





Interpretation: The scatterplot displays a circular, unorganized cloud of points with an empirical lag-1 correlation of \(r_1 \approx -0.033\). Extremely wet years (such as 1883 with 40 inches) can be followed by average or dry years. Past rainfall provides virtually no linear predictive power for next year’s rainfall; this series behaves like independent white noise.



3.2 Case 2: Industrial Chemical Process (color)
The color dataset tracks color intensity across 35 consecutive batches in a chemical manufacturing process.


Code
data(color)

plot(
  color,
  ylab = "Color Property",
  xlab = "Batch",
  type = "o",
  pch = 16,
  col = primary_col,
  main = "Chemical Process: Batch Color Property"
)
grid(col = grid_col)








Figure 3: Exhibit 1.3: Time series plot of color property for consecutive manufacturing batches.





We now plot batch color \(Y_t\) against the previous batch \(Y_{t-1}\):


Code
plot(
  y = color,
  x = zlag(color),
  ylab = "Current Batch Color",
  xlab = "Previous Batch Color",
  pch = 19,
  col = point_col,
  main = "Color vs. Previous Batch Color"
)
grid(col = grid_col)

r1_color <- cor(color[-1], zlag(color)[-1])
abline(lm(color[-1] ~ zlag(color)[-1]), col = accent_col, lwd = 2)








Figure 4: Exhibit 1.4: Scatterplot of batch color property versus previous batch color.





Interpretation: Unlike rainfall, neighboring batches show positive temporal persistence with a correlation of \(r_1 \approx 0.55\). Low values tend to follow low values, and high values follow high values, making first-order autoregressive modeling appropriate.



3.3 Case 3: Annual Abundance of Canadian Hare (hare)
The hare dataset contains annual counts of Canadian hare abundance over 31 years (1905–1935).


Code
data(hare)

plot(
  hare,
  ylab = "Abundance",
  xlab = "Year",
  type = "o",
  pch = 16,
  col = primary_col,
  main = "Annual Abundance of Canadian Hare"
)
grid(col = grid_col)








Figure 5: Exhibit 1.5: Annual abundance of Canadian hare (1905–1935).







Code
plot(
  y = hare,
  x = zlag(hare),
  ylab = "Current Year Abundance",
  xlab = "Previous Year Abundance",
  pch = 19,
  col = point_col,
  main = "Hare Abundance vs. Previous Year"
)
grid(col = grid_col)

r1_hare <- cor(hare[-1], zlag(hare)[-1])
abline(lm(hare[-1] ~ zlag(hare)[-1]), col = accent_col, lwd = 2)








Figure 6: Exhibit 1.6: Hare abundance versus previous year’s abundance.





Interpretation: The time plot exhibits distinct cyclical behavior (predator-prey population cycles) with strong positive autocorrelation (\(r_1 \approx 0.7\)). Neighboring years change smoothly rather than abruptly.



3.4 Case 4: Monthly Average Temperatures in Dubuque, Iowa (tempdub)
Monthly average temperatures (in \(^\circ\text{F}\)) recorded in Dubuque from 1964 to 1975.


Code
data(tempdub)

plot(
  tempdub,
  ylab = "Temperature (°F)",
  xlab = "Year",
  type = "o",
  pch = 16,
  col = primary_col,
  main = "Monthly Temperatures in Dubuque, Iowa"
)
grid(col = grid_col)








Figure 7: Exhibit 1.7: Monthly average temperatures in Dubuque, Iowa (1964–1975).





Interpretation: This series exhibits deterministic annual seasonality with period \(s = 12\) months. Januarys are consistently cold (around \(15^\circ\text{F}\)), while Julys are consistently warm (around \(75^\circ\text{F}\)).



3.5 Case 5: Monthly Oil Filter Sales (oilfilters)
Monthly dealer sales of specialty oil filters for construction equipment manufactured by John Deere (1983–1987).


Code
data(oilfilters)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Standard plot
plot(
  oilfilters,
  type = "o",
  pch = 16,
  ylab = "Sales",
  xlab = "Time",
  col = primary_col,
  main = "Standard Line Plot"
)
grid(col = grid_col)

# Modified plot with seasonal letters
plot(
  oilfilters,
  type = "l",
  ylab = "Sales",
  xlab = "Time",
  col = "gray60",
  main = "Plot with Month Symbols"
)
grid(col = grid_col)
points(
  y = oilfilters,
  x = time(oilfilters),
  pch = as.vector(season(oilfilters)),
  col = accent_col,
  cex = 0.9,
  font = 2
)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))








Figure 8: Exhibits 1.8 & 1.9: Oil filter sales with standard lines (left) and monthly plotting characters (right).





Interpretation: While the company manager initially believed sales were non-seasonal, labeling observations by month reveals that winter months (January, February) consistently see high dealer stock replenishment, whereas autumn (S, O, N, D) sales drop substantially.

title: Chapter 1 · Introduction to Time Series
text:
4 Solutions to Chapter 1 Exercises

4.1 Exercise 1.1: Los Angeles Rainfall Plots

Use software to produce the time series plot shown in Exhibit 1.2 on page 2. The data are in the file named larain.



Code
data(larain)

plot(
  y = larain,
  x = zlag(larain),
  ylab = "Annual Rainfall in Year t (inches)",
  xlab = "Annual Rainfall in Year t-1 (inches)",
  pch = 21,
  bg = primary_col,
  col = "black",
  main = "Exercise 1.1: Exhibit 1.2 Reproduction"
)
grid()












4.2 Exercise 1.2: Chemical Process Color Property

Produce the time series plot displayed in Exhibit 1.3 on page 3. The data file is named color.



Code
data(color)

plot(
  color,
  ylab = "Color Property",
  xlab = "Batch Number",
  type = "o",
  pch = 16,
  col = primary_col,
  main = "Exercise 1.2: Exhibit 1.3 Reproduction"
)
grid()












4.3 Exercise 1.3: Simulated Gaussian Random Process

Simulate a completely random process of length 48 with independent, normal values. Plot the time series plot. Does it look “random”? Repeat this exercise several times with a new simulation each time.

We simulate 4 realizations of length \(n = 48\) with \(e_t \sim i.i.d. \, N(0, 1)\) using explicit seeds:


Code
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(3.5, 3.5, 2.5, 1))

seeds <- c(101, 102, 103, 104)
for (i in seq_along(seeds)) {
  set.seed(seeds[i])
  wn_norm <- ts(rnorm(48))
  
  plot(
    wn_norm,
    type = "o",
    pch = 16,
    col = primary_col,
    ylab = "Value",
    xlab = "Time",
    main = paste("Normal Run", i, "(Seed:", seeds[i], ")")
  )
  abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "red")
  grid(col = grid_col)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))








Figure 9: Exercise 1.3: Four independent realizations of standard Gaussian white noise (n = 48).





Discussion: Although the underlying process is completely independent, individual finite sample realizations often show localized “runs” or pseudo-clusters (e.g. 3 consecutive values above 0). The human eye often tends to identify false patterns in purely random series.



4.4 Exercise 1.4: Simulated Chi-Square Random Process

Simulate a completely random process of length 48 with independent, chi-square distributed values with 2 degrees of freedom. Display the time series plot. Does it look “random” and nonnormal? Repeat several times.

A \(\chi^2(2)\) distribution has mean \(\mu = k = 2\), variance \(\sigma^2 = 2k = 4\), and is positively skewed (\(\text{Skewness} = \sqrt{8/k} = 2\)).


Code
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(3.5, 3.5, 2.5, 1))

seeds_chisq <- c(201, 202, 203, 204)
for (i in seq_along(seeds_chisq)) {
  set.seed(seeds_chisq[i])
  wn_chisq <- ts(rchisq(48, df = 2))
  
  plot(
    wn_chisq,
    type = "o",
    pch = 16,
    col = accent_col,
    ylab = "Value",
    xlab = "Time",
    ylim = c(0, max(wn_chisq) + 1),
    main = paste("Chi-Square (df=2) Run", i)
  )
  abline(h = 2, lty = 2, col = "black")
  grid(col = grid_col)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))








Figure 10: Exercise 1.4: Four realizations of independent Chi-Square (df = 2) white noise (n = 48).





Discussion: The plots are visibly non-normal: values are bounded below by 0 with frequent sharp upward spikes. However, they remain independent over time; high spikes do not predict subsequent spikes.



4.5 Exercise 1.5: Simulated Heavy-Tailed Student’s t Process

Simulate a completely random process of length 48 with independent, t-distributed values each with 5 degrees of freedom. Construct the time series plot. Does it look “random” and nonnormal? Repeat several times.

The \(t(5)\) distribution is symmetric with mean 0 and variance \(\frac{\nu}{\nu - 2} = \frac{5}{3} \approx 1.67\), but possesses heavy tails (leptokurtic).


Code
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(3.5, 3.5, 2.5, 1))

seeds_t <- c(301, 302, 303, 304)
for (i in seq_along(seeds_t)) {
  set.seed(seeds_t[i])
  wn_t <- ts(rt(48, df = 5))
  
  plot(
    wn_t,
    type = "o",
    pch = 16,
    col = point_col,
    ylab = "Value",
    xlab = "Time",
    main = paste("Student's t (df=5) Run", i)
  )
  abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "red")
  grid(col = grid_col)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))








Figure 11: Exercise 1.5: Four realizations of independent Student’s t (df = 5) white noise (n = 48).





Discussion: The series looks symmetric around 0, but exhibits occasional extreme isolated spikes (heavy tails). Crucially, the extreme observations are single events that immediately return toward the mean, demonstrating temporal independence.



4.6 Exercise 1.6: Dubuque Temperatures with Seasonal Symbols

Construct a time series plot with monthly plotting symbols for the Dubuque temperature series as in Exhibit 1.7 on page 6. The data are in the file named tempdub.



Code
data(tempdub)

plot(
  tempdub,
  type = "l",
  col = "gray50",
  ylab = "Average Temperature (°F)",
  xlab = "Year",
  main = "Dubuque Monthly Temperature with Month Symbols"
)
grid(col = grid_col)

# Add monthly letters (J, F, M, A, M, J, J, A, S, O, N, D)
points(
  y = tempdub,
  x = time(tempdub),
  pch = as.vector(season(tempdub)),
  col = primary_col,
  font = 2,
  cex = 0.85
)








Figure 12: Exercise 1.6: Dubuque monthly temperatures with month character symbols.





Discussion: The monthly labels illustrate that the cyclical waveform is strictly synchronized with the calendar year: J (January) always forms the trough (\(\approx 15^\circ\text{F}\)) while J (July) always forms the peak (\(\approx 75^\circ\text{F}\)).

title: Chapter 1 · Introduction to Time Series
text:
5 Chapter 1 Synthesis: Key Takeaways









Dataset
Sampling Frequency
Dominant Pattern
Temporal Dependence




larain
Annual
White noise
Uncorrelated (\(r_1 \approx 0\))


color
Batch
Short memory / Persistence
Moderate positive (\(r_1 \approx 0.6\))


hare
Annual
Multi-year population cycles
Strong positive (\(r_1 \approx 0.7\))


tempdub
Monthly
Deterministic annual seasonality
High periodic dependence (\(s = 12\))


oilfilters
Monthly
Winter surge / Autumn drop
Seasonal demand pattern




5.1 Fundamental Theoretical Insight
Never confuse the marginal distribution (shape across a histogram, e.g. Normal, Chi-square, Student’s \(t\)) with temporal dependence (correlation across time). A series can be highly non-normal yet completely independent, or perfectly normal yet strongly autocorrelated.

title: TP 02 · Fundamental mathematical concepts
text:
3 Derivation template
Copy this pattern under each exercise:

Assumptions: Define the process and the properties of the innovations.
Mean: Calculate \(E(Y_t)\) and check whether it depends on \(t\).
Autocovariance: Calculate \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_t,Y_{t-k})\) and check whether it depends only on \(k\).
Conclusion: State the stationarity result and justify it.
R check (optional): Simulate with a fixed seed; use it as a check, not as proof.
